title: How to Set Your 2027 Marketing Budget (Small Shop)
h1: Set a 2027 marketing budget that makes sense
meta: Stop guessing. Tie your 2027 marketing spend to cost-per-booked-job, not likes or impressions. A plain-English budget for a small contractor shop.
short: Budget off cost-per-booked-job, not vanity metrics. A simple way to decide what to spend.
statLabel: the only number your budget should track

body.answer: Set your 2027 budget off one number: what it costs you to book a job. Not likes, not impressions. If a channel books jobs cheaper than your profit per job, spend more. If it doesn't, cut it.
body.html:
Most contractors set a marketing budget by feel, or by whatever a salesperson talked them into. Then they can't tell you if it worked. Fix that for 2027. Budget off one number: cost per booked job.

Here's the whole idea. Add up what you spent on a channel. Count the jobs it actually booked. Divide. That's your cost per booked job. Compare it to your profit on a job. If the channel costs less than you make, feed it. If it costs more, kill it. Likes and impressions don't pay your crew.

body.h2: Do the arithmetic on each channel
body.answer: Spend divided by booked jobs equals cost per booked job. Run it for every channel you use so you can see which ones earn their keep.
body.html:
Say you spent $1,000 on a channel last quarter and it booked 5 jobs. That's $200 per booked job. If your average job clears $600 in profit, that channel is a machine — pour more in. If those same 5 jobs cost you $1,000 each, you're lighting money on fire.

Run this for Google ads, your profile, your site, referrals, lead sites — all of it. The channels that book jobs cheap get next year's money. For the full framework, read our contractor marketing budget guide.

body.answer: Owned assets — your Google profile, reviews, and site — usually book the cheapest jobs. Max those out before you spend a dollar on ads.
body.html:
Before you set an ad budget, max out the free channels. Your Google Business Profile, your reviews, and your website book jobs at basically no cost per lead once they're set up. That's the cheapest cost-per-booked-job you'll ever get.

Reviews do a lot of the work: most homeowners read online reviews before choosing a contractor, and most won't seriously consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal Local Consumer Review Survey). So stacking reviews is budget work, not fluff. Start with how to get more Google reviews.

body.h2: Watch out for lead mills and ask your accountant on taxes
body.answer: Be careful with shared-lead sites, and talk to your accountant about how marketing spend hits your 2027 taxes.
body.html:
Shared-lead sites sell the same lead to four shops, so your real cost per booked job is higher than the sticker price. Watch them closely. The FTC fined HomeAdvisor/Angi $7.2 million (FTC, 2023) over how leads were sold, so track your own numbers and don't take their word for the math.

One more thing. Marketing spend has tax angles — timing, deductions, what counts. That's not our lane. Ask your accountant. If you want a human to help you size the budget and pick channels, talk to Aaron.

faq.q: What percentage of revenue should a contractor spend on marketing?
faq.a: Forget percentages. Spend whatever books jobs below your profit per job. A channel at $150 per booked job on $600 jobs deserves more money regardless of what percent of revenue that is.

faq.q: How do I know my cost per booked job?
faq.a: Take what you spent on a channel and divide by the jobs it actually booked — not calls, not clicks, booked jobs. Track it per channel so you can compare.

faq.q: Can I write off marketing on my taxes?
faq.a: Usually marketing is a business expense, but the specifics depend on your situation. Ask your accountant — this isn't tax advice.
